opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it starts with a very simple observation, which is that the world itself is incredibly diverse. If you look at evolution, nature never converged on one body plan. You have octopuses, birds, ants, humans, each shaped by the environment and the task it needed to survive in. Form follows function, and the physical world presents an almost endless variety of functions.

Robots are going to be deployed into the same messy, three-dimensional world. A robot that works inside a surgical setting, one that inspects pipelines, one that harvests strawberries, one that helps an elderly person get out of bed: these have fundamentally different requirements for size, dexterity, strength, safety, and cost. I don't see why we would force all of them into a single humanoid shape, or even a handful of shapes. The humanoid is compelling, partly because our environments are built for human bodies, and I think it will have its place. But it's one point in a very large design space.

The other piece is that what has been truly missing isn't the body, it's the intelligence: spatial intelligence. The ability to perceive, reason about, and act in 3D space. If we get that foundational layer right, if models can genuinely understand geometry, physics, and how objects and agents interact, then that intelligence becomes much more embodiment-agnostic. That actually frees up hardware to diversify, because you're not handcrafting the brain for every new body. So I'd expect a Cambrian explosion of forms, sitting on top of a more shared understanding of the 3D world.

r001.rationale: The response says different tasks call for different robot requirements and forms, but it does not say that restricting robots to a few forms would be energy inefficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the answer really comes from looking at nature, and also from thinking about what a robot is actually for. If you look at biology, evolution didn't converge on one body plan. We have creatures that fly, that swim, that burrow, that climb trees, and each of those forms is shaped by the environment and the tasks the animal has to accomplish. Form follows function. A body is really a solution to a particular set of problems in a particular world.

Robots are going to be the same. A robot that works in a warehouse moving boxes has very different needs from one that assists a nurse in a hospital, or one that inspects a pipeline, or one that helps an elderly person get out of bed at home. Some of these need to be strong, some need to be gentle, some need to be very small, some need to be stable on uneven ground. There's no single geometry that is optimal across all of those.

Now, I know there's a lot of excitement around humanoids right now, and I understand why. Our world is built for human bodies, so a humanoid form can in principle slot into human spaces without redesigning the environment. I think humanoids will absolutely have their place. But I don't think they're the endpoint. The humanoid form is one point in a very large design space, and it carries a lot of constraints that come from our evolutionary history, not from engineering. Two legs are actually a pretty hard way to stay balanced. If you don't have to be human, why pay that cost everywhere?

The other piece, and this is where my own work comes in, is that I think the intelligence and the body are going to become much more decoupled than they've been historically. For a long time, every robot needed its own bespoke software because perception and control were so tightly tied to a specific hardware configuration. That's changing. As we build models that have a genuine understanding of the 3D world, of objects, of space, of physics, that spatial intelligence can be shared across many different embodiments. And once the intelligence is portable, the barrier to designing a new body drops dramatically. You're not starting from zero every time.

So I actually expect we'll see something like a Cambrian explosion. Lots of experimentation in form, lots of specialization, many of them coexisting. And honestly, I find that much more exciting than a world of identical machines. Diversity is how you cover the enormous range of things people actually need help with.

r001.rationale: The response says different tasks favor different robot forms and that no single geometry is optimal, but it does not state that restricting robots to a few forms would be energy inefficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the diversity comes from the diversity of tasks and environments. A robot that helps you in the kitchen has very different physical requirements from one that works on a farm, explores underwater, or moves things in a warehouse. The body matters: what you can reach, how you move, how you grasp something—all of that shapes what you can do.

There’s a good argument for humanoid robots because we’ve built so much of our world around the human body. But that doesn’t mean the human form is optimal for every task. Sometimes you want wheels. Sometimes you want a very small machine, or an arm that stays in one place.

So I would expect some commonality in the intelligence that powers these systems, while the physical forms remain quite diverse. A shared ability to understand the world doesn’t require everyone to have the same body.

r001.rationale: The response says different tasks and environments call for diverse robot forms, but it does not state that restricting robots to a few forms would be energy inefficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the diversity will come from the diversity of tasks and environments. A robot that works in a hospital has very different requirements from one that works on a farm, or in your kitchen. What does it need to reach? What does it need to carry? Does it need to move up stairs, or navigate uneven ground? Those questions shape the body.

The human form is compelling because so much of our world is designed around humans. But that doesn’t mean every robot needs two arms and two legs. If you’re solving a specific problem, a different form might be simpler and more effective. I would expect some common platforms, but also a lot of diversity as we discover what these machines can do.

r001.rationale: The response says different tasks and environments call for diverse robot forms, but it does not say that restricting robots to a few forms would be energy inefficient.
